title: A light for the little tent
intro: Mouse has tucked a blanket inside the tent. There’s a pillow, too, and a tiny place for muddy boots. But when the sun goes down, it gets awfully dark in there. Could you help make a little lamp?
question: If there’s a gap in one wire, will the little lamp still shine?
choices: I think it will go dark
discovery: The light needs a whole path through the battery, resistor, and LED. Opening one wire breaks that path. Closing it again lets the light shine, as long as the LED faces the right way and the batteries are working. The resistor stays in the loop to limit the current.
invitation: Give your lamp a home. A tent, a cave, or a tiny reading room? Make the paper setting your own, and show someone where the light’s path goes.

title: The fox’s secret flap
intro: Fox has made a cardboard flap with something shiny underneath. Close it, and a little light comes on. Open it, and the light disappears. There’s no magic hiding in the cardboard. Let’s find the part that makes the difference.
question: What will happen when the two pieces of foil stop touching?
discovery: The touching foil makes a connection in the light’s path. Separating it opens the circuit. That is what a switch does: it gives us a way to open and close a path on purpose.
invitation: Make a paper door with a handle of your own. Can it close the foil contacts reliably three times?

title: The squirrel’s material mystery
intro: Squirrel has brought a paperclip, a plastic lid, and a very serious expression. One of these might help a light shine. Another might leave it dark. Looking at the objects won’t tell us everything, so we’ll make a little tester and collect some clues.
question: Which object do you think could complete the light’s path?
discovery: A conductor allows enough current through our tester to light the LED. Many metals do this; dry plastic usually does not. A loose connection can also leave the light dark, so check the tester before deciding what an object tells you.
invitation: Choose a safe, dry mystery object with your helper. Predict its result, then let someone else investigate it.

title: Turn the little light around
intro: Rabbit has put the same tiny light into the same circuit twice. One way it shines. The other way it doesn’t. The battery hasn’t changed, and the resistor is still there. Could the light’s two legs be trying to tell us something?
question: Will the LED shine both ways around in this circuit?
discovery: An LED has two different terminals. In this circuit, it lights in one orientation and stays dark in the other. We call this polarity. Your helper checks the actual part and marks the terminals, because leg length alone can be misleading after trimming.
invitation: Design a tiny label that would help a friend remember the LED’s direction.

title: Two bright windows
intro: Mouse’s little house has two windows: one by the kitchen and one beside a stack of books. We’d like a light in each. But what if a wire comes loose in the kitchen? Let’s build two paths and see whether the reading light needs to go out too.
question: If one light loses its path, must the other one go dark?
discovery: These two branches share the battery but give each light its own complete path. Opening one branch can leave the other working. Each LED has its own resistor; we never make the two lights share a single current-limiting resistor.
invitation: Make two rooms and explain which connections they share and which belong to just one light.

title: A picture with a little glow
intro: Fox has drawn a woodland scene, but one detail is missing. Perhaps a cabin needs a window, or a star wants to peek through the trees. You can choose where the light belongs. Then we’ll find out how to keep the circuit working inside a picture.
question: Where could a light help someone understand your picture?
discovery: The picture and the circuit have to work together. Paper can tug on a wire, and a loose connection can interrupt the light’s path. Testing the finished picture in its display spot helps us notice problems that weren’t there on the table.
invitation: Change one part of the picture or its support. Show how your change makes the invention look or work better.

title: A firefly’s blinking message
intro: A tiny light on the board is blinking steadily. Squirrel wonders whether it could blink a little faster, like a firefly in a hurry. The board follows instructions, including how long to wait. Let’s change those waits and see what the light does.
question: What will shorter waits do to the blink?
discovery: The instructions repeat: light on, wait, light off, wait. Shortening both waits makes the pattern repeat faster. You changed the timing while keeping the same light and the same order of actions.
invitation: Invent a recognizable blink. Explain which waits you changed so someone else could recreate it.

title: A crossing for the tiny town
intro: Rabbit’s paper town has a crossing, three lights, and a queue of imaginary bicycles. The lights can take turns, but how long should each turn last? Let’s keep the order and change just one wait to find out what happens to the whole pattern.
question: If green stays on longer, will one whole pattern take longer?
discovery: A sequence has an order and a timing. We can keep red, green, and yellow in the same order while changing how long one light stays on. That longer green wait adds time to the whole cycle.
invitation: Choose a different wait for your pretend town and explain who it might help. This is a tabletop model, not a road signal.

title: The button at the workshop door
intro: Fox wants visitors to press a button when they arrive. A little light will let the workshop know someone is outside. The strange part is that the board calls a press LOW. How could a LOW reading make a light turn on?
question: What do you think the board reads when this button is pressed?
discovery: Our input is held HIGH by the board’s internal pull-up resistor. Pressing the button connects that input to ground, so it reads LOW. The code notices LOW and turns a different output HIGH to light the LED. The input and output have different jobs.
invitation: Build a paper flap that gently presses the same button. Can someone use it comfortably five times?

title: A softer lighthouse glow
intro: Mouse’s paper lighthouse has one lamp, but it doesn’t always need the same glow. Could we make it look softer without changing the light itself? The board can switch it on and off much faster than our eyes can follow.
question: Which setting do you think will look brighter: 64 or 192?
discovery: The board sends quick on-and-off pulses. More of each pulse spent on usually looks brighter; less time on looks dimmer. This is called pulse-width modulation, or PWM. It is not the same as supplying a smooth lower voltage.
invitation: Try a gentle glow for a paper lighthouse and explain what your chosen number changes.

title: A secret signal at camp
intro: Two short flashes shine across the pretend campsite. Then comes one long flash. Rabbit thinks it might mean ‘tea is ready,’ but Fox thinks it means ‘bring a blanket.’ Before we can send a useful message, we need a pattern someone else can recognize.
question: Could someone tell two messages apart by their timing?
discovery: A signal can carry a message when people agree what its pattern means. Short and long flashes give us different patterns to choose from. Testing with a partner tells us whether our message is actually easy to recognize.
invitation: Invent two messages and ask a partner to identify each three times. A silent light pattern is enough.

title: Wait for the firefly
intro: Squirrel’s finger is ready, but the little light is taking its time. Pressing early would be easy. Waiting for the actual signal is the interesting part. Let’s investigate how a game can tell a quick reaction from a guess.
question: Should a press before the light count as a reaction?
discovery: The game keeps track of whether it is waiting, showing the cue, or waiting for a release. An early press is a false start. The physical board reports an estimate that includes its button-handling delay, so it is useful for comparing trials rather than measuring exact human reaction time.
invitation: Try five fair turns. What changes with practice, and what might make the comparison unfair?

title: The fox’s cardboard jaw
intro: Fox has made a cardboard creature with a very long tail and a rather impressive jaw. Push the tail down and the jaw rises. But does it matter where you push? Let’s look under the decoration and find the simple machine doing the work.
question: Which push spot will make the same paper load feel easier to lift?
discovery: The cardboard arm turns around a pivot. Pushing farther away can make the same load easier to lift, but your hand travels farther too. That is a tradeoff. Real cardboard bends and pivots rub, so a difference that is too small to feel is still an honest result.
invitation: Turn your lever into an animal of your own. Show someone the pivot and the two push spots hiding in its design.

title: The squirrel’s drawing machine
intro: Squirrel turns a cardboard handle and a marker wanders across the paper. The marker has no motor. A few connected strips are guiding its movement. What do you think would happen if we changed one place where those strips join?
question: Will moving one joint change the marker’s path?
choices: It will be exactly the same
discovery: A linkage connects parts so that moving one guides the others. Its lengths and pivot positions shape the motion. Compare the same small handle movement before and after a change; a different input movement would make the comparison harder to explain.
invitation: Turn your traces into a picture, then point to the one joint that changed the drawing.

title: A leaf that waves hello
intro: Rabbit has cut out a paper leaf for the workshop window. It would be lovely if it could wave at visitors. A little motor called a servo can try to move to a requested position. Let’s see what two carefully chosen positions can do.
question: Will two different position commands make the leaf point different ways?
discovery: The board sends a control signal, and the servo tries to turn to the requested position. The servo has its own adult-prepared power supply. The light paper leaf must have room to move without catching or straining.
invitation: Keep the same checked positions and change a pause. What makes the greeting feel slower or quicker?

title: A dial for the puppet
intro: Fox’s paper puppet needs a way to point at things. A button offers a choice, but a dial can offer many positions in between. Turn a little here and watch a little movement there. How does the board connect the two?
question: What will happen as you turn the dial toward its other end?
discovery: The dial changes an input reading. The code maps that reading to a servo position inside the chosen range. Checking the low end, middle, and high end helps us see whether the input and movement fit together.
invitation: Give the puppet three things to point at. Keep its movement inside the helper-checked range.

title: A bridge for a paper boat
intro: Mouse’s paper boat is approaching the bridge, and its mast is a little too tall. The bridge needs to lift. Could a button ask a servo to move it while everyone keeps their hands clear of the hinge?
question: How could a button request a movement without pushing the bridge itself?
choices: The button has to touch it
I want to trace the steps
discovery: The button changes an input. The code chooses a position, and the servo moves the bridge. Following this chain helps us decide where to investigate if the bridge does not move as expected. A catching hinge needs a mechanical check, not a stronger command.
invitation: Make a paper boat for the river and explain what you would check if the bridge caught on something.

title: A creature with a wiggle
intro: This paper creature has something to say, but it has no words. Perhaps a slow turn means it is curious. Perhaps a quick greeting means it has spotted a friend. Squirrel wants to find out how much expression can come from the timing of a simple movement.
question: Could the same positions look different when the pauses change?
choices: The positions are all that matter
discovery: A movement sequence combines positions and timing. Keeping the checked positions while changing a pause lets us investigate timing on its own. People may read the gesture differently, so listening to a partner is part of the experiment.
invitation: Give your creature a greeting, then ask someone what they thought it was saying.

title: A cloud over the robot eye
intro: Rabbit slides a paper cloud across a tiny sensor. Nothing touches the sensor, but the numbers on the screen begin to change. Could this circuit help an invention notice a shadow? Let’s collect some readings before deciding what the numbers mean.
question: Will the readings get bigger or smaller when you shade this sensor?
discovery: The photoresistor changes resistance with light. In this particular divider circuit, brighter light usually gives a larger reading and shade a smaller one. The numbers describe this circuit in this room; they are not a calibrated light measurement.
invitation: Make a sliding paper cloud and compare readings before, during, and after its shadow.

title: A lamp for the reading nook
intro: Mouse is halfway through a book when the reading nook starts getting dark. A light sensor can notice a change, but somebody still has to decide what ‘dark enough’ means. Let’s use actual readings to choose a rule for the lamp.
question: How could we choose a useful number for turning the light on?
discovery: A threshold is a dividing point for a decision. We choose one between our measured light and shade readings, then test it. A different room or sensor position may need a different threshold, which is why calibration belongs to the actual build.
invitation: Make a shade for the nook. Did it change when the lamp came on?

title: An echo by the cardboard wall
intro: Fox holds up a cardboard wall in front of a sensor with two round openings. The sensor sends out sound and listens for its return. Could the length of that journey tell us how far away the wall is?
question: Will a closer wall send the echo back sooner?
discovery: Sound travels to the target and back. A longer trip generally takes more time. Some targets return a poor echo, and sometimes no usable echo arrives. A missing reading means we do not know the distance; it does not mean zero.
invitation: Compare flat cardboard with soft fabric at the same distance. Which gives clearer evidence?

title: A clue for the little cart
intro: Squirrel’s tabletop cart is edging toward a cardboard wall. A flashing light could give us a clue about the distance. But what should happen when the sensor cannot find the wall at all? A useful invention needs a way to admit when it doesn’t know.
question: What could faster flashes tell us in this model?
choices: We need to agree on a rule
discovery: The code translates a distance reading into a flashing pattern. Closer valid readings produce faster flashes. With no usable echo, the model does not know the distance. An off light cannot promise that the way is clear. This tabletop model is not a safety device.
invitation: Invent a separate sign for ‘I don’t know’ and explain why your model needs it.

title: The warm little bead
intro: Rabbit has found a tiny sensor shaped like a bead. Your helper has checked and insulated it so that only its dry covering can be touched. Could gentle warmth from a hand change its reading? We’ll need patience, because a small change can be difficult to spot.
question: What might happen to the reading as the checked bead warms gently?
choices: It may stay hard to distinguish
Let’s watch a group of readings
discovery: This thermistor changes resistance with temperature. The readings can reveal a trend, but they are not yet temperatures in degrees. Room conditions, insulation, and timing affect what we observe. If the change is too small to distinguish, say so.
invitation: Draw the pattern of your readings, including any uncertainty. No heating devices are part of this activity.

title: The treasure box’s light clue
intro: Mouse wants to know when the treasure box opens. Light slips inside as the lid rises, and a sensor might notice. But would that clue work in a dark room? Let’s find out what the invention really detects.
question: Does opening a box always make the inside brighter?
discovery: The sensor notices light, not the lid itself. The box alert turns on above a chosen threshold. In a dark room, opening the box may not change the reading enough. Testing different conditions helps us discover that limitation.
invitation: With power off and your helper’s help, try another sensor position and repeat the same opening test.

title: What’s inside the mystery box?
intro: Fox has brought a cardboard box with a little tab sticking out. Push the tab gently, let go, and watch. Something inside is making it move, but the lid is still closed. Can you imagine two different explanations before asking to peek?
question: When you let go of the tab, what do you think it will do?
discovery: ‘The tab came back’ describes an observation. ‘An elastic band pulled it’ is one possible explanation. Other mechanisms could give a similar result. Repeating an outside test helps us compare ideas, but an observation alone may not prove exactly what is inside.
invitation: Sketch two possible insides. Ask your helper before opening the prepared model, then compare your ideas with what is there.

title: The woodland repair shop
intro: A little lamp has arrived at Squirrel’s repair shop, and it won’t shine. Your helper knows that it worked before hiding one safe fault. There are several possible clues, but changing everything at once would spoil the mystery. Which part would you inspect first?
question: Can a dark LED alone tell us whether a wire is loose or the LED is backwards?
choices: Yes, darkness tells us the fault
No, both could make it dark
discovery: An observation is not yet a diagnosis. A useful repair test separates possible causes. Change one thing with power disconnected, ask your helper to check, then compare the result with your prediction. A failed attempt can still narrow the mystery.
invitation: Tell your repair story, including an idea that did not work. What evidence finally helped?

title: Can you copy that movement?
intro: Rabbit has watched a cardboard machine make a lovely little movement. Your pieces are different sizes, but perhaps they could make something similar. We’ll study what goes in, what comes out, and which joints guide the motion.
question: Could different link lengths produce a similar output movement?
discovery: Reverse engineering starts by studying what a working object does and how its parts might produce that behavior. A new design can make a similar movement while differing in travel, wobble, or stability. Compare the same input motion to see those differences.
invitation: Choose one thing to improve, change one dimension or prepared pivot position, and test again.

title: A handle that helps
intro: Mouse’s paper flap is easy to see but awkward to open. A loop might help, or perhaps a wider tab. Different makers may prefer different shapes. Let’s build two possibilities and listen carefully to the person who tries them.
question: Will the same handle feel easiest for everyone?
discovery: Engineering includes deciding whom a design should help and how to tell whether it helps. A bigger grip may suit one person, while another prefers a different shape. Feedback gives us evidence for a change instead of making us guess what someone needs.
invitation: Improve one handle after your partner’s test, then compare three gentle openings before and after the change.

title: The six-material invention
intro: Fox has cleared a space on the workbench. There’s cardboard, paper, tape, string, a covered fastener, and a marker. What could these become? Choose a small problem, decide what success would look like, and make a first version that teaches you something.
question: Which part of your idea would be most useful to test first?
discovery: A prototype is a version we build to learn from. A falling flag or slipping link gives us useful evidence. Keep the goal the same, change one feature, and test the next version in the same way so you can explain what improved.
invitation: Show both versions and the evidence for your change. What would you try if one material disappeared from the kit?

title: The workshop’s invention day
intro: The workshop table is filling up with little houses, moving creatures, and drawings of ideas still being worked out. Rabbit has saved a place for your invention. You don’t need a perfect result to tell an interesting story. What did you try, and what did it teach you?
question: What would help someone understand how your invention works?
choices: A story about what I changed
discovery: An engineering story connects an idea with evidence. Showing a first attempt, an unexpected result, and a revision helps someone understand your decisions. A drawing or an unfinished invention can tell that story too.
invitation: Invite a listener to ask a question. Keep names and private details off the display, and choose what you’d like to investigate next.
